opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think the biggest change is that communication has to become much more deliberate.

In an open-source community, a lot of coordination happens almost implicitly. Everything is public: the issues, the pull requests, the design discussions. If you want to know what someone is thinking, you can read the thread. Decisions often emerge through consensus, or through whoever writes the code first. There's a kind of natural meritocracy. Nobody is formally in charge, so you persuade people with good code and good arguments. That works well when the goal is clear, like "make inference faster" or "support this new model," because the community is aligned on the technical direction.

A company is different. You have to make decisions that aren't purely technical: who to hire, which customers to prioritize, how to spend money, what *not* to build. Those can't all be resolved in a GitHub thread. And many of these conversations happen in private, so the shared context you get for free in open source isn't there anymore. You have to create it on purpose.

So among the founders, we've had to learn to be much more explicit. We talk more often, and more directly, about disagreements. In open source, if two people disagree, sometimes the project can support both approaches, or someone just forks it. In a company you can't really fork yourselves. You need to reach a decision, commit to it, and make sure everyone actually commits, not just nods.

Another part is clarifying roles. In the community, people wear many hats. Someone reviews code one day, answers user questions the next, then writes a blog post. As founders we've needed to say clearly: you own this area, I own that one, and here's how we hand things off. That clarity actually reduces friction, because you're no longer stepping on each other's toes or assuming someone else is handling something.

And there's a cultural balance we try to keep. We came from open source, and that spirit of transparency and respect for technical arguments is valuable. We don't want to lose it just because we're a company now. So we try to keep that openness internally, writing things down, sharing reasoning, while accepting that a company needs faster, more accountable decision-making than a community does.

In a way, it's like moving from a loosely coupled distributed system to one where you need stronger consistency guarantees. You pay some overhead in communication, but that's the price of moving together in one direction.

r001.rationale: The response says founders communicate more often and directly so they can decide, commit, and move together in one direction, tying closer communication to alignment around a shared direction.

fable-5.1.text:
In an open-source community, communication is almost by definition asynchronous and public. Everything lives in GitHub issues, pull requests, Slack threads that anyone can read. People are scattered across time zones, most of them have day jobs, so you can't expect a reply in an hour. The upside is that the whole discussion is written down, and decisions are made in the open. If someone proposes an architectural change, the reasoning sits in the PR description and the review thread, and six months later a newcomer can trace exactly why we did it that way. Writing well is the core skill. I spent a lot of time learning how to explain a design clearly in text so that someone I've never met can understand it and push back on it.

When you move to a company, a few things change at once. First, the founders are now in the same place, or at least on the same calendar, so a lot of communication collapses into synchronous conversations: standups, whiteboard sessions, a quick call. That's faster, but it also means decisions can evaporate. Someone says something in a meeting, three people nod, and nothing gets written down. So one thing we've been deliberate about is keeping the open-source habit of writing things down even when we could just talk. Design docs, decision logs, that kind of thing. Otherwise the people who weren't in the room, including our community contributors, lose the thread.

Second, there's a new layer of conversation that didn't exist before: business. In the community, the only question was "is this the right technical change?" Now we also have to talk about priorities, customers, hiring, money. Those conversations are harder because they're less objective. A benchmark tells you whether a kernel is faster. Nothing tells you definitively whether to spend the next quarter on feature A or feature B. The founders have to build a different kind of trust for that, one where you can disagree about judgment calls without it feeling personal.

And third, there's the question of what stays public. In the community, there was nothing to hide. In a company, some discussions are genuinely internal: a customer's roadmap, a hiring decision. We have to consciously decide what goes to the public channels and what doesn't, and be careful that the public project doesn't start feeling like it's run by an invisible group making decisions somewhere else. That's the real risk. The community trusted us because they could see how we worked. We want to keep as much of that visible as we can, and be honest about the parts that have to move behind closed doors.

So in short, the founders talk more, talk faster, and talk about more things. The challenge is to not let the convenience of a quick conversation erode the discipline of writing things down and deciding in the open, because that discipline is what made the project work in the first place.

r001.rationale: The response says founders communicate more often and synchronously because they share a place or calendar, but it does not attribute closer communication to pursuing a shared goal.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest change is that communication has to become more explicit. In an open-source community, people can contribute based on their interests, and a lot of coordination happens around a particular issue or pull request. When you become a company, the founders need to agree on priorities: what we’re building, who we’re building it for, and how we’re spending our time.

You can agree on the technology and still have different expectations about the business. So I think you need to talk about those expectations early, including who makes which decisions and how you resolve disagreements. That doesn’t mean making every conversation formal. It means being comfortable saying, “I see this differently,” before that difference becomes a problem.

r001.rationale: The response says company founders need more explicit communication to agree on priorities and expectations, but it does not attribute closer communication to pursuing a shared goal.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest change is that you can’t rely on everyone naturally being on the same page anymore. In an open-source community, people can work on what interests them, and a lot of communication happens through issues, pull requests, and technical discussions. In a company, the founders also have to agree on priorities: what we’re building, who we’re building it for, and what we’re willing to postpone.

So communication has to become more deliberate. If we disagree, we need to understand whether it’s a technical disagreement or whether we’re making different assumptions about the business. And once we make a decision, we need to communicate it clearly to the team. I’d want to preserve the openness of the community while being clearer about responsibility and how decisions get made.

r001.rationale: The candidate says company founders must align on priorities and communicate more deliberately, but does not clearly attribute closer communication between them to pursuing a shared goal.
